item.title: The Trump administration just cut down a century’s worth of history at a D.C. golf course
item.description:
Workers removed more than 500 trees over the weekend at a Washington, D.C., golf course that President Donald Trump is working to remodel. It happened like many of his other design projects around town: suddenly and without permission.

Preservationists asked a judge Sunday to halt the Trump administration after it removed 529 trees Saturday at East Potomac Park, a golf course managed by the National Park Service, and on Monday, a judge called the removal “inexcusable.”

The course is home to elms, oaks, pines, and willows, as well as some of the 3,000 Japanese flowering cherry trees gifted by the government of Japan in 1912. Together they told the story of golf’s rise in America from a mostly treeless game on the U.S. coasts to a sport known for its big, lush vegetation. Now, just like that, a century’s worth of landscape design history has been torn up.

The removal happened “faster than anticipated,” according to the lawsuit, and the Trump administration didn’t meet its obligations under the National Environmental Policy Act, attorneys representing the D.C. Preservation League and a pair of local golfers said in a filing seeking an emergency action to pause further tree removal.

“‘Pulling a fast one’ has become the model this administration uses to circumvent the laws intended to protect the environment and D.C. landmarks,” Abbe D. Lowell, a founding member of Lowell & Associates, which is representing the plaintiffs along with Democracy Forward and Democracy Defenders Fund, said in a statement. “It did so with the East Wing and the Kennedy Center, and we are continuing our effort to stop them before they succeed in destroying D.C.’s historic public golf course.”

A brief history of parkland courses

East Potomac Park sits on a small island in the Potomac River, just south of the National Mall. Its earliest known vegetation consisted of tall grass and willow trees, most of which were cleared to design the first golf course in 1917. Over the years, more trees were added to adapt to changing tastes, according to a 2017 cultural landscape inventory of the course conducted by the Urban Heritage Project from the University of Pennsylvania’s Stuart Weitzman School of Design.

The first course at East Potomac Park was designed by golf course architect Walter J. Travis, who cleared the fairways of most willows but kept some existing trees along the course’s perimeter to separate the front and back nine. A new style of golf course design in the 1920s called parkland style, however, meant more trees would eventually be planted over the years.

As golf grew more popular and moved inland, parkland courses came to be known for their big, mature trees. The popularity of televised golf tournaments beginning in the 1950s and ’60s only made lush, green, gorgeous park-like backdrops that more appealing, according to the inventory, like the Masters Tournament in Augusta, Georgia, with its trees and plants imported from around the world in bloom.

At East Potomac Park, the Civilian Conservation Corps planted cedar trees in 1939 and additional trees in the 1960s and ’70s, including crab apple trees. The 2017 inventory also counted large wolf trees, large willow oaks, and a large American elm.

Some trees were planted for reasons of gameplay, not just aesthetics. The park’s miniature golf course, for example, was designed around a limited number of trees that function as hazards, and the park’s White Course has few trees and open fairways, making it popular with less competitive players.

The 2017 inventory noted that the park needed some care, including clearing invasive vines and trees that were were damaging some of the cherry trees. It also said that a “piecemeal nature of planting” had resulted in “a variety of mature trees and shrubs scattered throughout the landscape” that had no overall harmony.

A “surprise demolition”

But those suing Trump’s Interior Department and National Park Service say the administration’s tree razing went far above routine maintenance or a thoughtful pruning, and that the administration had even removed healthy, mature oaks and maple trees.

“Unleashing a surprise demolition razing over 500 historic trees in this public park and claiming it is part of maintenance from a dated, years-old landscaping plan is yet another brazen, lawless power grab that has become routine for the Trump administration,” Democracy Defenders Fund executive chair Norm Eisen said in a statement.

Trump’s planned makeover of the park (he had rubble from the White House’s East Wing demolition taken there) is part of a larger takeover of the federal government golf course system. Trump is reportedly offering his Trump International Golf Club West Palm Beach in Florida as an official U.S. government golf course for presidents that his family’s company would continue to operate.

Like the rings of a tree tell its story, the landscape design of East Potomac Park told a story of a game that grew up to appreciate the value of mature trees and ample vegetation as it became more popular. With the Trump administration’s sudden tree removal, part of that history is now gone.

item.title: Congress wants to keep AM radio in every new car
item.description:
In the era of streaming music and satellite radio, traditional broadcast stations are easy to overlook. AM radio, in particular, has fallen out of favor with younger drivers. So it’s perhaps no surprise that some automakers have begun dropping it from new vehicles. Congress, however, wants to put a stop to that.

Last month, the U.S. House of Representatives passed H.R. 979, the “AM Radio for Every Vehicle Act of 2025.” The bill is now on the Senate’s legislative calendar and has broad bipartisan support. The Senate also has a companion bill, S. 315, which cleared committee last year and is awaiting a floor vote.

While AM radio is dominated by political talk shows, religious programming, and sports, it still draws a sizable audience. The National Association of Broadcasters (NAB), which supports the congressional effort, says more than 80 million Americans listen to AM each month.

The group describes AM radio as “a platform for locally produced content that is relevant to their audience and speaks to their unique cultural and linguistic needs.” It also notes that AM stations have historically provided an entry point into radio ownership for racial and ethnic minorities.

Automakers, meanwhile, are grappling with tariffs and rising component costs, and looking for ways to trim expenses. Removing AM radio wouldn’t shave hundreds or thousands of dollars off a vehicle’s price, but it could offer modest savings.

Electric vehicle makers face another challenge: The technology that powers EVs can interfere with AM radio reception.

“The high-voltage electrical systems in EVs generate electromagnetic interference that, according to the Center for Automotive Research, ‘distorts AM radio signals, affecting the listening experience for drivers and passengers.’ In other words: really staticky,” said John Bozzella, president and CEO of the Alliance for Automotive Innovation, in 2024 congressional testimony. “It’s not possible to eliminate that interference, and techniques to reduce interference add weight and mess with battery range and would cost an estimated $3.8 billion.”

Bozzella also argued that requiring AM radio amounted to a government mandate with no public safety justification.

Supporters of the legislation dispute that argument. AM stations play a significant role in the nation’s emergency alert infrastructure, including a FEMA-supported network of radio stations equipped to continue broadcasting during disasters.

Bozzella’s position was echoed by the then-president and CEO of the Consumer Technology Association, who wrote in a letter to the editor of The Washington Post that “a federal mandate that every car comes equipped with an AM radio in 2024 and beyond is like mandating that they come equipped with ashtrays or 8-track players.”

Still, traditional radio may have more life left in it than skeptics think, even as music streaming subscriptions approach 1 billion worldwide.

As more Americans return to the office, radio has benefited from renewed interest. Edison Research’s “Share of Ear” report, released in July, found that AM/FM radio accounted for 62% of ad-supported audio listening among adults, compared with just 6% for Spotify’s ad-supported service. In cars, AM/FM commanded an even larger share of ad-supported audio listening: 82% among adults 18 and older.

Whether the Senate will vote on the AM radio bill before November’s midterm elections remains unclear. And despite its bipartisan support, its prospects at the White House are uncertain.

The auto industry may oppose the measure, but it has some influential backers beyond the broadcasting industry, including the American Farm Bureau Federation, AARP, and a coalition of public safety organizations.

item.title: Elon Musk quietly becomes the biggest donor in the midterms in a bid to save Republicans
item.description:
Elon Musk, the world’s only trillionaire, has quietly become the biggest known donor in this year’s midterm elections, doling out more than $276 million since July to try to save Republican majorities in Congress.

The numbers, first reported by The New York Times ahead of this week’s federal filing deadline, were confirmed by Andrew Romeo, a spokesperson for Musk’s super PAC.

The money includes $158 million given to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC supporting Republican Senate candidates, one of the largest known political donations in American history, according to the Times.

Another $76 million went to America PAC, a Musk super PAC, which has once again built out a major turnout operation like the one it used to help elect President Donald Trump by knocking on doors in 2024.

Musk also provided $10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, a group that supports the Republican nominee for Senate in Texas, Ken Paxton. The race has been a major focus of Musk’s efforts.

It’s a dramatic turnaround since last May, when Musk said he intended to cut back on future political spending. “I think I’ve done enough,” he said at the time.

Despite the cash infusion, Musk has generally kept a lower profile than in 2024, when he appeared onstage next to Trump at rallies, and in the early days of the president’s second term, when he led the Department of Government Efficiency.

He had a falling out with Trump while leaving his government post, but the two have since reconciled. Trump presented Musk with the National Medal of Science last week.

Musk’s net worth has fluctuated around the trillion-dollar line this year based on changes in stock prices, but he topped $1 trillion again last week according to Forbes magazine.

Republicans have a gaping financial advantage over their Democratic counterparts—a disparity that has been a rare bright spot for a party that is bracing for major potential losses amid deep voter frustration over the president’s performance, stubbornly high prices, and the unpopular war with Iran.

They have been using the money to blanket the airwaves in the race’s final stretch.

“These robust investments have allowed the GOP apparatus to get its message out so Republicans can have a fighting chance to defy history,” Romeo told the Times.

Democrats responded to the news by accusing Republicans of using vast amounts of cash to mask their shortcomings.

“Republicans are hoping to buy these elections, injecting tens of millions into races to try and outrun their unpopular candidates, unpopular president, and unpopular economy,” said Lauren French, a spokesperson for Democrats’ Senate Majority PAC.

—By Jill Colvin, Associated Press

item.title: Subterranean Warfare - An Urgent DoW Need Without An Owner
item.description:
The DoW urgently needs to organize its scattered subterranean warfare assets into a single unified organization. Ideally, a Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager (DRPM) for Subterranean Warfare, reporting to the Deputy Secretary of War. (The Department already uses this model for unmanned systems, critical weapons and Golden Dome.) This group would have three portfolios: Subterranean Resilience, Subterranean Sensing and Subterranean Defeat. The office would integrate validated requirements, experimentation, testing, acquisition, and fielding.

Subterranean Resilience

During the 2026 Iran conflict, Iranian ballistic missiles and low-cost drones hit U.S. installations across eight Middle Eastern countries. Hundreds of buildings and structures were damaged or destroyed. The Navy’s Fifth Fleet headquarters in Bahrain was among the installations hit hard. Iranian weapons damaged one E-3 airborne early-warning aircraft and five KC-135 tankers on the ground in Saudi Arabia. (The official inspector-general report documents the damage.) Despite thousands of successful interceptions, the attacks exposed the vulnerability of concentrated, above-ground assets.

The rapid redeployment of the B-1s from RAF Fairford in the UK after warnings of an Iran-linked threat (reported as a possible drone attack) made the point: unsheltered concentrated high-value aircraft are vulnerable even way outside the theater.

The assumptions the U.S. has made about air superiority, missile defense, aircraft dispersal, building hardening, and the survivability of concentrated forward bases were all flawed. While we were prepared for ballistic missiles and hostile aircraft, drone swarms combined with ballistic missiles saturated and got through our defenses.

Washington’s reaction has been to invest billions of dollars in counter-drone and missile defense systems. Yet public budget documents reveal no comparable effort to put vulnerable aircraft, fuel, command-and-control nodes, and munitions out of harm’s way – sheltered, underground (or in space). (Agile Combat Employment, dispersal, hardening, deception, shelters, and rapid runway repair were never designed for a combined drone and missile onslaught.)

The Pentagon has recognized for decades that underground facilities are among the most effective ways an adversary can blunt U.S. conventional superiority. It described that problem explicitly in 1999. Gaza and Ukraine should have made it abundantly clear.

China, Russia, North Korea, and Iran use underground facilities, dispersal, hardening, and deception to make their own high-value assets harder to find, assess, and disable. We need to underground assets that cannot be quickly replaced: command posts, comms nodes, ammunition, fuel distribution points, repair facilities, key power systems, maintenance spares, and high-value aircraft or drones. The department needs an integrator that coordinates resilience across the Military Departments, Joint Staff, combatant commands, defense agencies, and intelligence community and provides Subterranean Resilience.

However, resilience is only one part of subterranean warfare.

Subterranean Sensing and Defeat

The U.S. needs to know where adversaries' underground facilities are located, and the internal layout of those facilities. Today, these bespoke exquisite systems for tunnel detection, robotic mapping of accessible tunnels, Hard and Deeply Buried Targets (HDBT) characterization, and target defeat are siloed in organizations scattered across the DoW. Most of these systems still require boots on the ground. Once a target is found, Combatant Commands need an integrated system that can characterize and destroy these targets, without first gaining physical access. Today, for the deepest facilities that means bombing from the air. Iran is the case in point.

Background. Iran's route to a nuclear weapon is by enriching uranium. Natural uranium is composed of 0.71% uranium-235 (U235) and it’s only the U235 that is used to build a bomb.

Iran uses centrifuges to separate U235 and increase its concentration (enriching it.) One centrifuge won’t do much, but connecting thousands of centrifuges together into cascades and running them for months can produce pounds of U235.

Iran’s underground nuclear enrichment site at Natanz had well over 10,000 centrifuges installed across dozens of cascades, and their Fordow nuclear enrichment site was built for 16 cascades, roughly 3,000 machines. Before the June 2025 strikes, Iran’s three declared enrichment facilities contained more than 20,000 centrifuges in 125 full-sized cascades.

The rough estimate needed for one Iranian nuclear weapon is ~100 lbs of U-235 at 60% enrichment or 55 lbs of U-235 at 90% enrichment (modern designs use less.) The difference is important, the lighter the weapon the easier it is to fit on a missile.

At its peak (Feb 2025 to June 2025) Iran’s cascades were delivering ~86 lbs of uranium enriched to 60% which is about 50 lbs of U-235 per month, which is just under one potential weapon every month. (Most weapons use U235 enriched to 90+% because that permits a smaller, more reliable design. Getting to that level in Iran might take days or weeks running the cascades, but building it into a weapon would still be needed.)

Deeply Buried Targets Versus Bunker Busters. One of the stated goals of the U.S. strikes on Iran was to remove their capacity to build nuclear weapons. This required the U.S. to destroy their deeply buried underground nuclear enrichment sites. The largest conventional bomb in the U.S. military’s arsenal is the 30,000-pound GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator, carried by the B-2 Bomber. A 2019 description said it could reach targets as far as 200 feet underground (its actual effectiveness depends on geology, concrete, facility design, entry points, and the use of multiple weapons). The Iranians knew this and built their nuclear enrichment sites underground. The Fordow site is ~260 to 300 feet under limestone and dolomite. The Natanz site is 25 to 160 feet underground, protected by a 25-foot concrete shield. (But public estimates are over the place.)

Iran declared Isfahan as an enrichment complex to the IAEA the day before the June 2025 strikes; inspectors never got inside it, therefore its depth and geology are unknown, but speculation is that the enrichment complex is 260 to 330 feet underground. Another suspected enrichment facility is in Pickaxe Mountain, where the exact depths, geology, are unknown but estimates put the facility 250 – 330 feet below the summit. Both Isfahan and Pickaxe were Iran’s shift toward "deep mountain basing" to escape the reach of conventional military strikes.

In June 2025 in Operation Midnight Hammer U.S. B-2 bombers dropped 14 GBU-57 bombs on top of Fordow and Natanz. At Isfahan (Esfahan) more than two-dozen submarine-launched Tomahawks hit tunnel entrances and surface targets. In March 2026, strikes at Natanz hit its entrance.

According to the Institute for Science and International Security, the 22,000 centrifuges at Natanz, the Natanz pilot plant, and Fordow are almost certainly wrecked. What may have survived is the enriched uranium, the spare parts, and the people, and that is the problem. The International Atomic Energy Agency estimated (in June 2025) that Iran had about 970 pounds of uranium enriched to 60%; it has since lost track of where it is. Iran's known uranium conversion capability at Isfahan was damaged, which it needed to turn the stockpile of enriched uranium into a weapon, and there is no public evidence that enrichment has resumed at Natanz, Fordow or Isfahan. We never hit Pickaxe Mountain or the Isfahan enrichment facility with the GBU-57. The strikes have set Iran back, but no one knows for how long.

While the GBU-57 MOP cannot cleanly punch through solid rock, the debate has shifted from an absolute physical destruction calculation to a functional denial calculation—meaning the military's goal would be to seal Iran's nuclear assets in a mountain tomb rather than blowing them up directly.

Did We Succeed? Our stated goal was to prevent Iran from rapidly rebuilding the capability to build nuclear weapons, but there’s no certainty that we did that. Repeated airstrikes may have damaged the buried enrichment plants, but we can’t prove it or account for the buried enriched uranium inside. The fact is that it’s extremely difficult to see how much damage the bombs did to Hard and Deeply Buried Targets (HDBTs) from the air, and without inspectors on the ground, knowing for sure is guesswork. Putting boots on the ground would carry enormous costs and risks. Negotiating the removal and inspection of weapons grade uranium would depend on Iranian cooperation and a way to verify we got it all. All bad choices.

There is another emerging option: autonomous drilling equipment.

Subterranean Sensing and Defeat. It’s not hard to imagine that with enough boots on the ground the U.S. could secure a landing zone, fly in drilling equipment and have crews drill hundreds of feet vertically or thousands horizontally to either place sensors and/or explosives. The U.S. has had organizations building specialized equipment and training for breaching tunnels in Combatant Commands and scattered across the DoW for years (DTRA, DARPA, Army ERDC and CAVES and CZ5 programs, SOCOM, Sandia and the Army's half-billion-dollar underground-training push (2018) and ATP 3-21.51 Subterranean Operations.) One can even imagine that there are teams already trained and equipment ready to go. And one can equally imagine the Iranians are waiting for them.

What’s new is autonomous drills that could provide post-strike bomb damage assessments and/or destroy Hard and Deeply Buried Targets (HDBTs) without seizing the site. They might be inserted covertly; more likely they'd need air cover while they work.

The combination of AI, robotics and autonomy moves this from science fiction to the possible.

Anduril, The Boring Company, Exodigo, Phoenix Boring, Earthgrid and Traysar are possible candidates to deliver these systems. There are likely others as well.

(Disclosure: after my first blog about undergrounding critical assets, I invested and have a financial interest in companies in this space.)

Surface survivability and subterranean sensing and defeat are no longer one Service's problem, and they won't be solved by a single system or an incremental fix. Something fundamentally disruptive has changed in the nature of asymmetric warfare and there’s no going back. While we’re actively chasing immediate solutions (Golden Dome, JIATF-401, et al), we need to rethink the nature of force protection, and military and civilian infrastructure protection.

The U.S. needs a coherent protection and survivability strategy across the DoW and all sectors of our economy. This conversation needs to be not only about how we do it, but how we organize it, how we budget and pay for it, and how we rapidly deploy it.

item.title: The Sanctions We Cannot Afford
item.description:
On the evening of Friday, October 9, the Treasury published General License 135. It authorizes the “sale, delivery, offloading and importation” of Russian diesel until April 7, 2027, and does not specify a buyer, a seller, or a quantity. The President provided the quantities after a call with President Putin: more than 300,000 tons “immediately,” 500,000 in November, and millions more if Russia’s refineries allow. The first shipment amounts to less than a day of American consumption. The shipment comes from a country that barred its own diesel exports in July and, in the last quarter, imported the fuel for the first time. AAA put the national average for diesel that day at $6.28 a gallon.

The license is valid for six months. The law beside it allows nine days. On September 18, the President signed a sanctions act that the Senate had passed 86-11. By October 18, it requires duties of up to 500 percent on Russian goods and duties of up to 100 percent on every export to the United States from any of the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or natural gas that knowingly purchases again. The first duty covers petroleum products, and so the diesel the Treasury has just licensed. A third law, passed in 2022 and never repealed, still bars Russian petroleum from American ports; the license does not mention it. Washington must penalize Russia’s customers nine days after licensing itself to become one.

For six weeks in these pages, I have argued that the United States is assembling the instruments of great-power competition without deciding who commands them. This week, the pattern reached the oldest instrument of economic warfare, the sanction, and it was not only an American pattern.

On October 7, the European Union’s ambassadors agreed on their 22nd package of sanctions against Russia. They removed one Russian company at Estonia’s request because it supplies the rare earths that an Estonian plant refines for European magnets. Two days later, in Beijing, the European trade commissioner announced an understanding under which China will moderate its exports of hybrid cars to Europe. In return, Beijing will continue to process European companies’ rare-earth and magnet licenses through what both sides call a green channel. The notice suspending China’s licensing rules for American buyers still expires on paper on November 10, eight days before the President is due in Shenzhen. The United States received no such channel.

China’s rare-earth controls are administered by a single ministry, which this week rewarded Europe while leaving the United States waiting. That is an exception used as an instrument: a favor granted in exchange for a concession, and revocable. The American and European exceptions were of another kind. They were relief from sanctions the governments had imposed themselves, granted because the price of diesel or a factory’s feedstock had become intolerable. An exception of that kind is information. It tells Moscow and Beijing the price at which the pressure on them will be lifted.

Each of the week’s decisions had a reason its government could defend. Diesel at more than six dollars a gallon before winter is a real problem, and so is a processing plant in a frontline state of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. But a sanction lasts only as long as its author can go without what it forbids.

The difficulty is that each decision was made by the office responsible for a single problem. The Treasury issues the license; the President sets the duties, and the Trade Representative adjusts them afterward. The fuel Russia has promised comes from refineries Ukraine is striking, so every Ukrainian strike now reduces the diesel Washington has announced, and Moscow has a commercial reason to ask the United States to restrain Kyiv. The President had already asked Kyiv in September to “take it easy on the refineries,” and President Zelensky called the license “a weak decision by strong partners.” No single authority beneath the President is charged with weighing one of these decisions against another before it reaches him. Each office did its work, and the claim that prevailed was the one with the nearest deadline.

The United States has faced this problem before. In July 1943, after a public quarrel between the board planning economic warfare and the agency financing it, President Roosevelt abolished the board. By September, he had placed economic warfare, lend-lease, and foreign relief under a single Foreign Economic Administration. He did so in the middle of a war because instruments that pull against one another need someone with the authority to rank them.

The duties due on October 18 are the place to begin, and they will be easy to read. A real duty on Russian goods and on Russia’s customers restores the sanction, and taxes the diesel Washington asked for. A nominal rate satisfies the statute and confirms the license as the policy. A waiver says so outright. In the last two cases, Russia’s customers may conclude that buying is safe, and Beijing that American pressure has a price that can be quoted in advance.

Avoiding that takes two things the West has not arranged. The first is a single authority who can rank the claims before they reach the President and hold every office to that ranking: someone who decides whether the sanction yields to the price of diesel or the price of diesel yields to the sanction. The second is provision. A sanction is a siege, and a siege is won by the side that can wait. A government that means to forbid a thing should first establish what it will need from the adversary while the prohibition lasts, then stockpile it, find it elsewhere, or grant the exception at the outset on its own terms.

If you advise on these decisions, ask for the ranking before the duties are signed and for the provisions before the next sanction is drafted. Otherwise, Moscow and Beijing will read October 18 as a schedule of American needs, with the dates on which they fall due.

item.title: What Beijing Calls Open, Washington Should Call an Operation
item.description:
China is about to run the largest influence operation in history. It will not have to run it. The world will download it.

Our research team at Vanderbilt spent months inside the internal documents of GoLaxy, a Beijing firm with ties to the Chinese state. It built a machine for shaping opinion in other countries: A.I. that generates personas, amplifies the stories Beijing wants believed and buries the ones it does not. It was used in Hong Kong. It was used in Taiwan. That is an influence operation built by hand, one persona at a time.

Now consider what happens when it does not need to be built at all. If Chinese open-weight models — the ones anyone can download, modify and run on their own machines — become the foundation the world builds on, the Party's framing of Taiwan, Tiananmen, Xinjiang and Beijing itself ships inside every product that sits on top. No personas. No campaign. Just the default answer, everywhere. GoLaxy would look like a rehearsal.

Here is the part that should stop Washington cold. Chinese models are about to be everywhere, and American strategy is what is putting them there.

Washington is deciding whether to let frontier development run while clamping down on powerful open-weight models whose safeguards can be stripped away. Restrictions would not kill demand for a cheap model a company can download and make its own. China is standing at the counter with exactly that.

We talk about the A.I. race as if it has one finish line. It has two. The first is for frontier capability: who builds the most advanced models. American companies lead today. The second is for reach: whose models become the foundation under thousands of products. Chinese firms may be building the advantage there. The first brings concentrated scientific, economic and military power. The second decides whose systems become the workhorses of ordinary life, and that reach shapes what people know.

American frontier models such as Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini are closed: you use them on the company's servers, and the company can cut off access. Chinese developers compete by releasing cheap open-weight models that companies can run on their own, with no provider to answer to.

This has already started. Airbnb relies on Alibaba's Qwen in its customer-service agent. Qwen even briefly powered a tool for searching proposed regulations on the Federal Register website. Amazon says thousands of customers have deployed DeepSeek through its cloud. In every case the interface is American. The model underneath is not.

Chinese developers operate under Communist Party rules about what may be said. Those rules shape which questions the models answer, which facts they omit and how they frame sensitive subjects. Open weights can be retuned, but scrubbing built-in defaults is expensive, and most companies will tune what matters to their business rather than check how a model handles every political subject. If a cheap Chinese model sits under thousands of products, its habits travel with it — into research tools, classroom software and fact-checkers — and the person on the other end never knows.

Beijing already believes this. When Meta released its open-weight Llama models, Chinese regulators worried that a foreign model could "poison" China's A.I. ecosystem with information the Party censors. Washington should take seriously a vulnerability Beijing recognized first.

None of this makes the open-weight safety problem smaller. It makes it bigger. Once a powerful open-weight model is out, its developer cannot recall it. Its safeguards can be stripped and the model turned toward cyberattacks, biological weapons or worse. Testing requirements, liability rules and release restrictions are needed. But a Chinese open-weight model carries the same dangerous capabilities as an American one, and no American rule touches it.

Constrain American developers and leave foreign weights untouched, and demand shifts toward Chinese models. Washington ends up regulating the companies it can see while deepening its dependence on the ones it cannot.

Washington could ban the Chinese models. But that means telling Americans which information technology they may use — and here lies the irony: the openness that protects Americans from domestic censorship may leave them exposed to systems built under Chinese censorship.

TikTok offers a glimpse of the stakes. More than 150 million Americans use it, and more than 50 million regularly get news there. Add DeepSeek or Qwen to generate the content TikTok’s algorithm selects and distributes, and China could supply both the information and the system that delivers it to an enormous audience.

The United States therefore faces a trilemma. It wants to prevent the uncontrolled release of dangerous A.I. capabilities. It wants to preserve Americans' freedom to choose their technology and information. And it wants to avoid dependence on models shaped inside an authoritarian system. It cannot fully secure all three.

Honest regulation starts by admitting that. Before restricting an American model, ask which model developers will pick instead. Domestic and foreign models distributed in the United States should face the same tests and the same rules. And companies that build products on a foundation model should have to say whose model it is.

A.I. leadership is two things: the capability of a country's best models, and the reach of the models embedded in ordinary life. A.I. risk is two things as well: what a powerful model might do, and what a ubiquitous one tells people is true. GoLaxy showed what Beijing does with a machine for shaping belief. Open weights are how it gets one in every pocket. And right now, Washington is holding the door.

Mr. Goldstein and Mr. Benson are professors at Vanderbilt University who specialize in national and international security.

item.title: Afghanistan produce thrilling rearguard to save Bangladesh Test
item.description:
Sediqullah Atal’s marathon century and some inspired lower-order resistance inspired Afghanistan to a dramatic draw in the one-off Test against Bangladesh on Tuesday.

Opener Atal, playing only his third Test, batted for eight-and-a-half hours for his 332-ball 111 before number nine Qais Ahmad hit an unbeaten 49 in Abu Dhabi.

Having started the final day on 132-3, Afghanistan survived to finish on 346-8, from a total of 142 overs, after being set a nominal 479-run target to win.

When Atal fell to a close-in catch off left-arm spinner Taijul Islam soon after tea with the score at 281-7, Bangladesh were in sight of victory.

But Qais and fellow tail-ender Yamin Ahmadzai (19 off 85 balls) batted for 110 deliveries in a valiant 45-run stand for the eighth wicket to resist Bangladesh’s spinners.

Even when Ahmadzai fell to Mehidy Hasan Miraz, Bangladesh had five overs to enforce a win but Qais and number 10 Zia-ur-Rehman hung on, although not without drama.

There were two missed run-out chances in the final session and a dropped catch, while Qais gave his team-mates watching from the boundary some heart-stopping moments.

The leg-spinner mixed solid defence with a penchant for dancing down the pitch, even hitting the second ball of the last over for six.

The Bangladesh players were less than impressed with Qais when he went down with an apparent hamstring injury and received treatment after playing a forward defence with 10 minutes remaining.

With a famous draw already secured, he hammered the final delivery of the match deep over midwicket for another maximum, falling to the turf in celebration.

Pacer Ebadot Hossain took 3-50 and off-spinner Miraz finished with 3-73, but it was not enough for Bangladesh.

Bangladesh skipper Najmul Hossain Shanto praised Afghanistan’s resilience.

“It is disappointing not win, but Afghanistan played brilliantly,” said Shanto. “I expected the spinners to come into the match. They tried but Afghanistan played very good cricket.”

Sediqullah earlier reached his century with a boundary off Hasan Mahmud, becoming the first Afghanistan batter to reach three figures in the fourth innings of a Test.

Hashmatullah Shahidi also scored 36 and helped Atal defy the Bangladesh bowling, but holed out to mid-on attempting a big shot down the ground, just seven minutes before tea.

Ismat Alam batted for 60 deliveries for his four — scoring his first run off his 44th delivery — before Miraz had him caught by Shanto.

With under two hours left, Bangladesh were finally rewarded with Sediqullah’s wicket as the left-hander pushed a turning delivery from Islam and a thick edge was well caught at short-leg by Tanzid Hasan.

But the exploits of Ahmadzai, Qais and Zia ensured the Afghans had the last say.

item.title: Maaz Sadaqat’s journey from Peshawar’s streets to Pakistan’s T20I spotlight
item.description:
Maaz Sadaqat could hardly have asked for a more emphatic introduction to international T20 cricket. After scoring a brisk half-century in only his third Pakistan outing, against Sri Lanka, the 21-year-old left-hander followed it with a breathtaking 96 off 51 balls in the second match, helping the national side register their highest men’s T20I total on home soil and clinch the series with an 82-run victory.

The two innings came on the back of a remarkable Caribbean Premier League campaign in which Maaz struck two centuries for Jamaica Kingsmen, including one in the final.

He made 112 off 49 balls in the eliminator before scoring 114 off 58 deliveries in the title decider. Although Jamaica lost the final, his performances had established him as one of the most exciting young batters in the tournament.

His innings against Sri Lanka have now brought that promise to a wider audience. Sunday’s knock featured six fours and seven sixes, taking Pakistan to 215-3 and equalling the record for the most sixes by a Pakistan batter in a men’s T20I innings.

Maaz fell four runs short of a maiden international century, but by then he had already helped Pakistan secure an unassailable 2-0 lead in the three-match series.

After Maaz’s 96, former Pakistan captain Mohammad Rizwan recalled on social media how the young batter had visited his home in Peshawar as a boy, accompanied by his elder brother, Haroon, with the ambition of one day representing Pakistan.

“It feels like yesterday when a young boy came to meet me in my Peshawar home with his brother Haroon, carrying a dream of one day playing for Pakistan,” Rizwan wrote on X, adding that seeing Maaz in the national shirt had brought him immense happiness.

The message offered a glimpse into the journey behind the sudden international attention, featuring a progression from tape-ball cricket in Peshawar to age-group cricket, domestic competition and, eventually, performances that could no longer be overlooked.

Born in May 2005, Maaz grew up playing cricket on the streets with plastic and tape balls. His elder brother, a first-class cricketer, helped introduce him to organised cricket after he completed his matriculation, taking him to Ashnaghar Cricket Club.

“I was a school kid and was hitting big sixes in my first club cricket game and everyone was super impressed,” Maaz had earlier recalled in a video posted by the Pakistan Cricket Board. His family subsequently encouraged him to attend trials, opening the way into the board’s pathways programme.

He progressed through district and regional under-19 cricket for Peshawar and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, finishing among the leading run-scorers in youth competitions before representing Pakistan at the 2021 Under-19 Asia Cup and the 2022 Under-19 World Cup. The experience gave him an early grounding in competitive cricket, but the transition to senior level would require more than the ability to strike the ball cleanly.

Maaz made his first-class debut for Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in the 2022-23 Quaid-e-Azam Trophy. He soon demonstrated that his attacking instincts could translate into the longer format, scoring 91 in one of his early matches. He also gained experience overseas, making his List A debut for City Club in Bangladesh’s Dhaka Premier Division in 2023.

Raffatullah Mohmand, his regional head coach and a former Pakistan player, was among those who helped guide his development. He recommended Maaz for the Bangladesh opportunity after the youngster impressed in Peshawar, believing he deserved greater exposure.

“Apart from being a quick learner and skilled cricketer, Maaz’s success also lies in in-depth preparation of all the challenges fronting him,” Raffatullah had said.

According to the coach, Maaz had begun observing and speaking to experienced players, including Rizwan, Iftikhar Ahmed and current Pakistan Sahibzada Farhan, from his teenage years, applying what he learned from them to his training and preparation. That willingness to learn, Raffatullah suggested, had helped accelerate his progress.

The first major glimpse of Maaz’s potential on a national stage came in the Pakistan Super League in May 2025. Making his debut for Peshawar Zalmi against Islamabad United, he walked in with his side in trouble at 38-3 while chasing 144. Rather than allowing the situation to dictate his approach, he counterattacked, scoring 55 off 33 balls in a match-winning partnership of 102 with Babar Azam.

Babar remained unbeaten on 53, while Sadaqat’s contribution earned him the Player of the Match award. For the young batter, sharing a partnership with one of Pakistan’s leading players was a moment of personal significance.

“With Babar at the other end, I felt no pressure and I turned to my natural game, acquiring more belief,” Maaz had said. “That time also helped me realise how much I have trained all my life to get here and do well.”

The innings appeared to announce the arrival of a promising new talent. Yet the attention it generated soon faded amid the demands of a crowded domestic calendar and the steady competition for places in Pakistan’s white-ball sides.

Maaz’s next breakthrough came later that year at the ACC Men’s Asia Cup Rising Stars in Doha. Representing Pakistan Shaheens in November 2025, he delivered an outstanding all-round campaign that made it difficult for selectors to ignore him.

He began with an unbeaten 96 off 54 balls against Oman and then produced one of the tournament’s defining performances against India ‘A’, taking two wickets for 12 runs before hitting an unbeaten 79 off 47 balls to help Pakistan Shaheens win by eight wickets. He finished as the tournament’s leading run-scorer with 258 runs in five innings at an average of 129, while taking seven wickets. He was named Player of the Tournament.

The performances were significant not simply because of the runs and wickets, but because they showed Maaz’s capacity to influence a match in more than one discipline. His left-arm orthodox spin offered an additional option, while his batting demonstrated that he could attack quality opposition without losing sight of the situation.

The Rising Stars tournament placed him firmly in the conversation around Pakistan’s future white-ball players. His subsequent engagements with Pakistan Shaheens, including overseas tours, provided further experience against different conditions and bowling attacks.

His next PSL campaign, however, was less transformative. Playing for Hyderabad Kingsmen in earlier this year, Maaz featured in 12 matches and scored 260 runs at an average of 23.63 and a strike rate of 178.08.

His highest score was 64, and he registered two half-centuries, hitting 27 fours and 16 sixes. The team reached the final, but Maaz’s season did not produce the same defining headline as his debut for Zalmi or his subsequent performances in the Caribbean.

The numbers nevertheless reflected a batter who continued to score quickly, even if he was not yet converting his starts into the kind of substantial innings that would make him a regular subject of national debate. His challenge remained to marry his high scoring rate with greater consistency.

Maaz had already taken another important step in March 2026, when he made his One-day International debut against Bangladesh.

In the second ODI, he scored 75 off 46 balls and took three wickets for 23 runs, earning the Player of the Match award. He finished the three-match series with 99 runs and three wickets.

The subsequent ODI series against Australia proved more difficult, with Sadaqat managing 35 runs across three matches. His early international record in the format offered encouragement, but it also illustrated the adjustment required to establish himself against senior opposition over a sustained period.

It was in T20 cricket, though, that he would soon make his most emphatic statement representing Jamaica Kingsmen in the CPL.

His selection for Pakistan’s T20I side, however, had a timeline of its own. The PCB announced him in the 15-member squad for the Asian Games in June, months before the CPL campaign. The tournament in Japan, scheduled for September and October, was to provide him with another opportunity to gain international T20 experience. His franchise commitments in the Caribbean meant that he was expected to join the national camp after the CPL concluded.

The Asian Games selection was an indication that the selectors were already monitoring his development. The CPL then offered a compelling demonstration of what he could bring to the format, before even as his international debut came in the Games, in which Pakistan took the silver medal.

While Maaz did not make a big impact in the two games Pakistan played in Japan, he impressed with a 50 off 29 balls as Pakistan chased down a target of 183 to take a 1-0 lead. Two days later, he went further, almost scoring a century.

The back-to-back performances brought together the strands of Sadaqat’s development — the fearless strokeplay first noticed in Peshawar, the lessons absorbed from senior players, the breakthrough in the PSL, the all-round success at the Rising Stars tournament and the proof of his power-hitting in the CPL.

At 21, he offers Pakistan an attacking left-handed batter who can also contribute with slow left-arm spin. His record so far also suggests that the next stage will be about consistency rather than discovery. The challenge is to turn eye-catching innings into a sustained run of performances and establish himself across formats, particularly in one-day cricket.

For now, Rizwan’s recollection of the young visitor to his Peshawar home provides an apt frame for Maaz’s rise. The dream of playing for Pakistan has become reality, and his first two T20Is have ensured that the conversation around him has moved well beyond the domestic circuit. The task ahead is to make this promising beginning last.

item.description:
Former two army officers, Lieutenant Colonel (Retd.) Debashish and Lieutenant (Retd.) Kazi Gulshan Ara, have been arrested by the Detective Branch of Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP).

Police stated that they were arrested under the Anti-Terrorism Act and Cyber Security Act cases.

According to police, they were arrested late last night during a raid in the capital. The operation was conducted by members of the Pallabi Zonal Team of DMP's Detective Branch. They were apprehended from a house in the Banani DOHS area at around 2: 30 AM.

Pallabi Police Station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Jalal Uddin told Prothom Alo that a DB police inspector has filed a case against the former army officers under the Anti-Terrorism Act and Cyber Security Act.

The case statement alleges that the arrested former army officers and their associates are involved in anti-government propaganda, fund-raising, and creating and promoting provocative digital content for violence on various social media platforms.

Additionally, they are accused of maintaining contact with former army chief General (Retd.) Aziz Ahmed and former Home Minister and top fugitive leaders through a platform named 'Unity Care Public Parliament' and are involved in conspiracies against the state.

The statement further claims that content was being created with the intent to incite violence and instability through a page called ''KalAjkal. com''. They are also accused of conducting and promoting various anti-state activities using social media.

According to the police's statement, they are accused of illegal financing with the intention of operating banned organisational activities and involvement in offences under various clauses of the Anti-Terrorism Act and Anti-Terrorism (Amendment) Ordinance, 2025. The statement mentions that since 5 August 2024, they have been conspiring against the government and Bangladesh alongside their associates and conducting slanderous propaganda.

Moreover, Lieutenant (Retd.) Kazi Gulshan Ara is accused of publicly expressing solidarity and loyalty to the then Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina with more than one and a half hundred retired army officers before the election on 27 November 2018. The statement also includes accusations of forming a committee named Bangladesh Army Council and spreading hatred among various classes and professions through the organisation.

Four-day remand granted

The court has granted a four-day remand for questioning the former army officers in this case. Dhaka's Metropolitan Magistrate Didarul Alam gave this order on Monday evening after a hearing. The state's lawyer Harun Or Rashid confirmed this information to Prothom Alo.

Before this, the investigation officer of the case, Inspector Sheikh Bashir Ahmed of DB's Cyber and Special Crime Division, presented former army officers Debashish and Gulshan Ara in court seeking a seven-day remand.

The remand application stated the necessity to identify and locate other accused individuals, verify the involvement of domestic and foreign individuals, recover digital evidence, search for any other websites or pages operated by the accused, and uncover the main mystery of the incident.

Around 5: 45 PM, defendants Debashish and Gulshan Ara were presented in the dock. The judge appeared shortly thereafter. The investigation officer then presented arguments in favour of the remand application, stating that they participated in WhatsApp meetings with the former Home Minister engaging in various plots to destabilise the country. Additionally, other various incriminating elements were found, prompting the remand request.

During this time, defendant's lawyer Abdullah Al Monsur requested to dismiss the remand application, stating that Lieutenant Colonel (Retd.) Debashish is the second accused in this case and claims against him are unacceptable. He questioned the rationale for the treason charge, stating that his crimes were not articulated in the remand plea.

And Gulshan Ara's lawyer Mohammad Moshiur Rahman argued that the accusation of attempting to destabilise the country by appearing on a talk show lacks substance as there is no mention of any destabilising statements made. The remand plea lacks grounds for the accused to be taken into custody.

Then, the state lawyer Harun Or Rashid argued for the remand, saying, "The accused have maintained regular contact with leaders and activists of the fallen government to destabilise the country. There is contact with local and international spies. We seek a seven-day remand to gather more information about their connections, sabotage activities, and their plans. "
After hearing from both sides, the court granted a four-day remand.

item.title: Durga Puja holidays: Banks, stock markets to remain closed for five consecutive days
item.description:
All scheduled banks in the country will remain closed for three days, from 20 to 22 October, for the upcoming Durga Puja festival. The following two days, Friday and Saturday, are weekly holidays. As a result, banks will remain closed for five consecutive days, from 20 to 24 October.

Bangladesh Bank issued a circular on Sunday announcing the directive. However, banks have been instructed to remain open on weekly holiday, Saturday, 17 October, as on a regular working day.

Durga Puja: Extended holiday gazette issued, what will remain open

Meanwhile, no trading will take place on the country’s two stock exchanges—the Dhaka Stock Exchange (DSE) and the Chittagong Stock Exchange (CSE)—during the bank holidays.

As stock market transactions are linked to banking operations, the stock markets will also remain closed for five consecutive days.

Although banks will remain closed from 20 to 22 October, limited banking services will continue in port and customs areas to keep import and export activities running.

5-day Durga Puja holiday; offices to remain open on preceding Saturday

The Bangladesh Bank circular further states that bank branches and booths in seaports, land ports and airports, including port and customs areas, must maintain limited operations during the Puja holidays to ensure that the country’s import and export trade continues uninterrupted.

Banks will take the necessary measures after consulting local administrations and port or customs authorities.

On 7 October, the Ministry of Public Administration issued a circular declaring holidays from 20 to 22 October for Sharadiya Durga Puja. It stated that all government, semi-government, autonomous, semi-autonomous and private offices would remain open on Saturday, 17 October.

item.title: 51 flights cancelled or suspended from Dhaka, 5,418 passengers affected
item.description:
The suspension of flight operations at various airports in Saudi Arabia has directly affected 51 flights operated by airlines serving Bangladesh through direct and transit routes.

Some flights have been cancelled, while others have been suspended. A total of 5,418 passengers scheduled to travel from Dhaka to various destinations in Saudi Arabia have been affected.

The Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh (CAAB) disclosed the information in a press release on Monday afternoon. The flights were cancelled or suspended between Saturday night and Monday afternoon.

According to CAAB, 12 of the 51 affected flights were direct services to and from Saudi Arabia, while the remaining 39 were transit flights. The direct flights included four operated by Biman Bangladesh Airlines, two by US-Bangla Airlines, three by Saudia and three by Riyadh Air.

Among the transit flights, 16 were operated by IndiGo, three by SalamAir, one by EgyptAir, nine by Emirates, five by Qatar Airways and five by flydubai.

According to the latest information from CAAB, the impact of restrictions on operations at Saudi airports is no longer limited to direct flights. Transit flights operated by various international airlines have also been affected, creating uncertainty for passengers' travel plans.

According to flight-tracking website Flightradar24, all flights bound for Riyadh have either been diverted or cancelled. A Reuters report said the decision followed a major attack on King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital on Saturday.

Reporting the suspension of flights at Riyadh's international airport, Reuters said airport authorities had advised passengers to contact their respective airlines before travelling to the airport and check the latest status of their flights.

US-Bangla cancels all Riyadh flights until 21 October

Private carrier US-Bangla Airlines said in a press release that all its flights on the Dhaka–Riyadh–Dhaka route had been cancelled until 21 October due to the closure of Riyadh airport. The affected flights are BS 381 and BS 382.

The airline said passengers would be informed once a revised flight schedule was finalised.

US-Bangla has requested passengers travelling to Saudi Arabia not to go to the airport for the time being. Passengers have been advised to contact the airline's sales centres or their travel agencies before visiting the airport to obtain updates on flight status, rebooking and other information. The airline apologised for the temporary inconvenience.

Expatriate workers from different parts of Bangladesh arrived at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka to travel to Saudi Arabia but were unable to leave because of flight cancellations and suspensions.

‘If I cannot return now, I will lose my job’

Abul Hossain was scheduled to fly to Dammam, Saudi Arabia, on a Biman Bangladesh Airlines flight at 2pm on Monday. He arrived at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka from Senbagh in Noakhali at around 10am to catch the flight, only to learn that it had been cancelled.

Hossain said he had been working in Saudi Arabia for six years and was currently employed as a tile mason in Riyadh. He had returned to Bangladesh on a three-month leave and had booked his return ticket three months in advance in line with his leave schedule.

The cancellation has left him worried about returning to his workplace.

“My leave has ended. If I cannot go back now, I will not be able to keep my job. Everything will become uncertain,” Abul Hossain told Prothom Alo.

Flight information board at the airport

Like Hossain, Md Moslem Talukdar also had his flight cancelled. His flight to Riyadh was scheduled for 12:10pm Bangladesh time. He had been waiting at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport since 10am when he learnt that the flight had been cancelled.

Speaking to Prothom Alo at around 3:30pm, Moslem Talukdar said, “My flight was scheduled for noon, but I could not leave. The airport is shut, and the flight has been cancelled. I am now checking whether I can travel on another flight. Otherwise, I will have to return home.”

He said he was due to join work at a shop in Riyadh.

Between 1pm and 4:30pm on Monday, Prothom Alo spoke to more than 15 passengers who had arrived at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport to travel to Saudi Arabia. Most of them were unaware that their flights had been cancelled, while some were waiting to see whether they could reach their destinations on alternative flights.

item.title: Iran says ‘deeply concerned’ over escalation between Houthis, Saudi Arabia
item.description:
Iran said Monday it was “deeply concerned” by escalating attacks between Yemen’s Tehran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia, after 14 people died in two days of strikes on Riyadh’s airport.
“We are deeply concerned about the developments taking place in the Arabian Peninsula,” foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei told a weekly press conference, adding that Tehran was ready “to help facilitate dialogue between the parties.”
A Houthi strike on Riyadh’s international airport on Sunday killed one person and wounded 11 others, a day after 13 died in the deadliest strike on Saudi soil in more than a decade.
“We absolutely do not want hostilities and war to continue between two Islamic countries,” Baqaei said, urging the parties to resolve the situation “through dialogue and engagement.”
The Houthis are part of the Iran-backed “Axis of Resistance,” a network of groups opposed to Israel that also includes Lebanon’s Hezbollah and Iraqi Shiite armed groups.

item.title: PM seeks Canadian support in energy, agriculture, climate finance
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Monday sought Canadian support in energy, agriculture and climate finance, while stressing the safe, voluntary and dignified repatriation of around 1.3 million Rohingyas to Myanmar as the only sustainable solution to the crisis.
He made the call when a Canadian delegation, led by its Secretary of State (International Development) Randeep Sarai, met him at his office at the Secretariat.
The meeting discussed strengthening bilateral relations, expanding economic cooperation and exploring new opportunities for a strategic partnership between Bangladesh and Canada, said PM’s Deputy Press Secretary Shahadat Hossain Shadhin.
Other key issues included technical and vocational education, food security, poverty alleviation and renewable energy.
On the Rohingya crisis, Tarique Rahman said Bangladesh is hosting around 1.3 million Rohingyas, putting considerable pressure on the country’s economy and environment while it continues to address its own economic and social challenges.
He said humanitarian assistance for the displaced people remained important, but their safe, voluntary and dignified repatriation is the only sustainable solution to the crisis, which originated in Myanmar and must be resolved there.
Randeep Sarai agreed on the importance of ensuring the peaceful, safe and dignified repatriation of Rohingyas.
The Canadian side expressed interest in cooperating with Bangladesh on energy supplies, particularly oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG), saying Canada could be a potential partner in these areas.
Bangladesh said it will consider the proposal positively.
Canada expressed interest in expanding cooperation in technical and vocational education and training (TVET) in Bangladesh.
The two sides also discussed cooperation in establishing nursing training institutions and developing skilled nurses. Canada already has activities in this sector and plans to expand them further, the meeting was told.
The meeting discussed opportunities to strengthen cooperation in the production and supply of agricultural commodities, including pulses and oilseeds.
Canada expressed interest in supporting Bangladesh’s efforts to ensure food security.
The Prime Minister was also briefed on existing programmes being implemented through the International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center (CIMMYT).
The two sides also discussed Bangladesh’s Farmers’ Card programme, under which the government plans to provide farmers with essential agricultural inputs, including fertiliser and seeds.
Tarique Rahman said the programme will help the government maintain detailed information on farmers, enabling better agricultural planning and more effective delivery of public support.
The meeting discussed how Bangladesh could benefit from Canada’s experience in data management and evidence-based planning in this sector.
Referring to World Bank data, the Prime Minister said integrating multiple food subsidy programmes, improving the aims of existing cash assistance schemes and linking them with the Family Card could help lift an additional 2.85 million people out of poverty.
He stressed the importance of economic self-reliance, saying his government is focusing not only on social protection but also on expanding income and employment opportunities to help people become self-sufficient.
The meeting discussed Bangladesh’s renewable energy initiatives, canal excavation and the programme to plant 250 million trees.
Randeep Sarai said Canada is interested in providing C$13 billion in global climate finance over the next five years, noting that Bangladesh could benefit from the funding.
Canada also expressed interest in supporting feasibility studies for development projects in Bangladesh.
The Canadian secretary of state praised Bangladeshis and people of Bangladeshi origin living in Canada for their initiative, skills and positive outlook.
He also informed the Prime Minister that two people of Bangladeshi origin are serving as members of the Canadian Parliament.
At the end of the meeting, Sarai invited Tarique Rahman to visit Canada.
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam, Prime Minister’s Adviser on Education, Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment Mahdi Amin, Press Secretary Saleh Shibly and relevant officials attended the meeting.
Canadian High Commissioner to Bangladesh Ajit Singh and senior officials from the Canadian side were also present.

item.title: America’s Military Has a GPS Problem
item.description:
“The Department of Defense’s (DoD) Global Positioning System (GPS) is the principal source of positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT) information for the U.S. military and civilian users. Due to DoD’s reliance on it, GPS also represents a potential single point of failure for DoD. We [the Government Accountability Office (GAO)] previously reported on DoD’s efforts to modernize GPS with a more jam resistant, encrypted, military-specific signal, referred to as military code (M-code), and we found that DoD is years away from fielding this capability after spending more than two decades and billions of dollars.”

That was the opening of a GAO letter sent last Wednesday to Congress accompanying a 58-page report titled PRECISION NAVIGATION SYSTEMS: Challenges Remain with Fielding New Capabilities, which explains the key role that GPS delivery of PNT data plays in this country’s military and civilian activities -- and the need to update the system.

The M-code secure, jam-resistant GPS signal is designed to be used by roughly 700 U.S. weapons systems deployed by Army, Navy, Marine Corps and Space Force services, but because of a limited supply of specialized microchip sets and production bottlenecks of other key elements, some M-code deployments have been pushed back to 2049, according to the GAO.

I will discuss this more below. Meanwhile, the U.S. military services continue to rely on legacy GPS receivers or alternative systems for PNT-guided operations. For example, the GAO report described “non-satellite-based PNT using data derived from internal or external sources of information to sensors, from geophysical sources, or from celestial sources (e.g., inertial measurement units, cameras or terrain sensors, magnetic or gravity sensors, and celestial sensors).”

First, a bit of GPS background and history supplied in part by the GAO.

GPS consists of three segments: a constellation of approximately 31 medium Earth-orbiting satellites, with at least 24 continuously broadcasting their position and time data; a ground control segment – Space Command’s Delta 8 at Schriever Air Force Base, Colo. -- for command and control of the satellite constellation; a user segment, comprising receivers used globally by military and civilians in aircraft, ships, land vehicles, precision-guided munitions, and handheld devices.

The user equipment receives signals from four GPS satellites and, with that transmitted data, instantly calculates the user’s location and precise time.

Although the U.S. Government created and continues to control and maintain GPS, it is freely accessible to anyone with a GPS receiver. There are three other similar global systems: Russia’s GLONASS was developed during the Cold War; the European Union manages Galileo, and China operates the BeiDou Navigation Satellite System.

Today’s U.S. GPS originated in 1973 when the Defense Navigation System, later named NAVSTARS GPS, was approved, primarily to guide ships. In 1978, the first GPS satellite was launched into orbit, with the full satellite complement not reaching initial operational capability until 1993. By then, it had been made available for civilian use as well as military, a decision made by President Reagan in 1983 after the Russian downing of Korean Air Lines Flight 007.

By the 1991 Persian Gulf War, the GAO report said, “GPS equipment was small and inexpensive enough to also be used on aircraft and other military vehicles. Since then, further advances, such as the development of even smaller microchip-sized receivers, have allowed GPS to provide precise PNT information for individual soldiers, munitions, smaller weapons technology applications, and civilian applications, like smart phones.”

Meanwhile, according to the GAO report, “GPS signals are being actively targeted by adversaries who seek to disrupt or deny GPS to U.S. warfighters. These threats include (1) jamming, (2) spoofing, (3) cyber, and (4) direct attacks on satellites or satellite infrastructure.”

DoD is mitigating jamming attacks “by installing specialized antennae -- referred to as controlled reception pattern antennae (CRPA) -- on weapon systems and munitions,” according to the GAO report, which added, “These antennae provide the ability to identify and filter out the jamming signals.”

Spoofing is being dealt with “in part by developing and installing receivers with M-code capability, which will provide more secure encryption,” the report said. As for cyberattacks, DoD is “ensuring that computer systems and networks are protected against cyber attacks that can target satellites and their associated ground control systems,” according to the GAO.

Since 2000, the Air Force -- and later the Space Force – have pursued a multibillion-dollar effort to modernize the existing GPS capability. The modernization effort included adding the more robust and more securely encrypted GPS military signal capability, known as M-code. It also included: 1) satellites that broadcast the M-code signal, 2) a ground system that controls both the existing and new M-code GPS satellites, and 3) user equipment to receive the M-code signals.

The first satellites capable of broadcasting M-code have been on orbit since 2005, with upgraded versions referred to as GPS III.

The launch of the GPS III third generation of 24 M-code satellites was completed on April 21 of this year, providing eight times the anti-jamming capability and four times the accuracy of previous iterations. “The next generation of satellites, known as GPS III Follow-on, or GPS IIIF, are in production by Lockheed Martin, and will begin launching as early as 2028,” according to a Space Systems Command press release.

However, it’s a different story with the new generation ground system, referred to as Next Generation Operational Control System (OCX). It began development in 2010 and was supposed to achieve transition to operations by June 2017. Instead, there were numerous technical problems and protracted delays. Costs rose from $3.7 billion to almost $7 billion or more, and in April 2026, DoD directed the Air Force to formally terminate the OCX program, according to the GAO report.

Despite the cancellation of the OCX program, then-Chief of Space Operations Gen. Chance Saltzman said in April the new ground control system needs to be prepared to support future GPS satellites, including GPS IIIF and beyond.

However, despite the OCX problems, the Space Force has been making upgrades to the existing GPS ground control segment through Lockheed Martin. Last week, an Air and Space Forces Magazine daily report said, “Since April, the Space Force has awarded Lockheed an additional $199 million…to support launch and command and control for GPS IIIF satellites…and to begin a full technology refresh of the GPS ground segment hardware and software.”

The final problems harming total GPS modernization – including delays and mounting costs – are best portrayed in the GAO report’s description of the military services’ development and procurement of separate receivers for the M-code data.

While development of the M-code-capable receiver cards has been led by the Space Force and Air Force, the eventual fielding of receivers to specific operational platforms, such as weapons, has remained the responsibility of the individual services.

According to the GAO report, “Currently, there are more than 50 priority weapon systems [considered in the GPS modernization programs]. The largest numbers of priority weapon systems are in munitions and aviation systems. The Navy has the highest number of systems, followed by the Army…Priorities for M-code modernization take into account the needs of the specific classified operational scenario as well as the expected life spans of the weapon systems involved. Weapon systems that are expected to no longer be in use around or before 2030 are not priority weapon systems.”

Congress mandated the PNT Oversight Council in the Fiscal Year 2016 National Defense Authorization Act, and DoD established it with the mission of overseeing the department’s GPS modernization portfolio.

However, as the GAO report explains, “Budget authority for key aspects of DoD’s PNT efforts remains under the control of the [separate military] services. This budgetary fragmentation complicates efforts to align interdependent PNT capability development and fielding efforts to ensure timely delivery to the warfighter.”

For example, the GAO found that despite recommendations from the PNT Oversight Council concerning inadequate Air Force funding for aviation receiver programs, “chronic underfunding” continued and the Air Force aviation receiver programs did not meet their development goals on their expected timelines.

“Pursuing modernized GPS and complementary PNT technologies to augment GPS,” the GAO report concludes at one point, “requires foresight and planning. Integration timelines for weapon systems are often lengthy, and schedules must be properly aligned for the development of such modernized PNT technologies and their integration into weapon systems. Additionally, these timelines for integrating new PNT technologies can be further complicated by the interdependence of systems. For example, the military services will likely upgrade some munitions to use M-code before the capability is integrated into weapon systems that fire those munitions.”

Since, as the GAO points out, the GPS system “is vast and touches almost all vehicles, ships, aircraft, precision-guided munitions, and dismounted personnel within the [Defense] Department,” I would say more DoD attention needs to be paid to getting this modernization back on track.
